name: radare2
why: A full reverse engineering framework for binaries, firmware, and running programs; a deep door into taking things apart.

brief.what_it_is: radare2 (r2) is a command-line reverse engineering framework: a set of libraries, tools and plugins for disassembling, analysing, emulating, debugging and patching binaries. It takes files, raw memory, or running processes (locally or via a remote gdb/windbg server) as input and produces disassembly, function lists, hexdumps, control-flow graphs, and edited binaries. The Homebrew package installs about twenty executables, including r2, radare2, rabin2, rasm2, rahash2, radiff2, rafind2, rax2, rarun2, ragg2, and the package manager r2pm.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says r2 is 'a complete rewrite of radare', and that the radare project 'started as a simple command-line hexadecimal editor focused on forensics'. The stated aim is to 'ease reverse engineering tasks' with a full-featured low-level command-line tool that can be scripted.
brief.how_it_works: r2 is a modular C framework. Its command-line shell takes short commands (for example aaa to analyse, afl to list functions, pdf to disassemble a function), and it can be scripted with an embedded JavaScript interpreter or through r2pipe from other languages. Architecture and file-format support, and extra features, come from plugins; r2pm installs third-party plugins such as the r2ghidra decompiler, r2frida, and the iaito Qt GUI.

commands_seen.context: Recommended install: clone the source repository before running the install script.
Runs the default acr+make+symlink installation from the cloned source.
Opens a file in read-only mode in the r2 shell (from the README usage example).
Inside the r2 shell, analyses the program (same as r2 -A).
Inside the r2 shell, lists all functions (README suggests trying aflt or aflm too).
Inside the r2 shell, prints a 32-byte hexdump at the current block.
Inside the r2 shell, seeks to main using its flag name.
Inside the r2 shell, prints the disassembly of the current function and then an ASCII-art function graph.
Searches r2pm plugin packages matching a word.
Updates the r2pm database and does a clean install of a package.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install: the README recommends building from git with sys/install.sh, and says meson/ninja (muon/samu also works) and make builds are supported. Uninstall the current build with make uninstall, or remove all system installs with sudo make purge. Windows builds need meson plus MSVC or MinGW, and use .bat scripts (preconfigure.bat, configure.bat, make.bat). r2 can also be installed via pip using r2env. Nix packaging is in dist/nix. Plugins are optional and are installed separately with r2pm. No accounts or API keys are mentioned.
brief.standout: The plugin ecosystem is wide: r2pm installs third-party tools, and the README lists decompilers (r2ghidra, r2dec, decai), a Frida I/O plugin, a Qt GUI, and a Ghidra bridge. Its architecture and file-format list is very broad, covering many CPUs including exotic and retro ones, and it can also mount several filesystems in userland.
brief.status: Maintained, by the evidence visible. The README says 'Current git master branch is 6.2.5, next release will be 6.2.6', and it shows CI, build and tcc status badges, a CII Best Practices badge, a Coverity scan badge, and packaging badges across many distros (Homebrew, Arch, Alpine, Fedora, Void, Termux, Snap, MacPorts). I did not see a release date or last-commit date, so I cannot say how recent the activity is.
brief.caveats: Licence: the core is LGPLv3, but the README warns that each plugin can have a different licence (check with r2 -Lj). Windows builds need meson with MSVC or MinGW. Source installs have build dependencies. The README's supported-platform list is long and not verified here. The homepage fetch returned almost no text (only the words 'Mastodon' and 'Radare Website'), so the project description rests on the GitHub README. Brew's own caveats field is empty.

judge.reason: A deep reverse-engineering framework that lets you dissect, emulate, debug, and patch binaries through a distinctive, scriptable command-line environment.

entry.title: radare2
entry.tldr: A command-line reverse engineering framework that disassembles, patches, debugs and scripts binaries, firmware and live processes from a terse shell.
entry.deeper_look:
radare2 (r2) opens a file, raw memory, or a running process, local or behind a remote gdb/windbg server, and gives you a shell for taking it apart. Short commands do the work: `aaa` analyses the program, `afl` lists functions, `pdf` prints the disassembly of one function, `agf` draws its control-flow graph in ASCII. You can also edit bytes and write the changes back, so it patches as well as reads.

It began, in the README's words, as "a simple command-line hexadecimal editor focused on forensics", and r2 is "a complete rewrite of radare". That history shows. The tool still thinks in offsets, bytes and blocks, and everything is a command you can type, script and repeat.

The Homebrew package installs about twenty executables, and most are small single-purpose tools that share the same libraries. `rabin2` reads file headers and symbols, `rasm2` assembles and disassembles, `rahash2` hashes, `radiff2` diffs binaries, `rafind2` searches, and `rax2` converts between number bases. They are useful on their own before you ever open the full shell.

The larger idea is that reverse engineering is a conversation with a binary, and a scriptable one. r2 can be driven by an embedded JavaScript interpreter or through r2pipe from other languages. Plugins add CPU architectures, file formats and features, and `r2pm` installs third-party ones such as the r2ghidra decompiler, r2frida and the iaito Qt GUI.
entry.install:
brew install radare2
# the README recommends building from git instead:
# git clone https://github.com/radareorg/radare2 && radare2/sys/install.sh
# plugins are optional and installed separately with r2pm

try_this.what_happens: Opens the ls binary read-only in the r2 shell, ready for poking.
Typed inside the r2 shell, analyses the whole program; afl then lists the functions it found.
Typed inside the r2 shell after seeking to a function (for example s sym.main), prints its disassembly and then an ASCII-art graph of its control flow.

entry.whats_unique: It is a whole toolkit built around one terse, scriptable command language, and its plugins cover many CPUs, including exotic and retro ones. It can also mount several filesystems in userland.
entry.caveats: The command language is cryptic and takes a while to learn, and each plugin can carry a different licence than the LGPLv3 core (check with r2 -Lj).
